newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Hardship said greater in northern Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Hardship said greater in northern Afghanistan.

text.p: People in Afghanistan's northern provinces face greater economic hardships than counterparts in Kabul and the month-on-month inflation rate in the region has soared to 140 percent, an aid agency official said on Monday.
"We thought (the capital) Kabul was terrible, but Mazar-i-Sharif (in the north) is worse," Jean Luc Piladini of the International Committee of the Red Cross in Kabul told reporters.

"It must be terrible to live in Mazar," he said of the base of the powerful Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who leads an alliance with the ousted government of president Burhanuddin Rabbani to fight the Taleban Islamic movement.
Ten northern provinces controlled by anti-Taleban factions are isolated from the rest of the country becasue of the fighting between the Taleban and the alliance.
The northern alliance has its own monetary system and currency, known as Dostum's banknotes, which are not valid in two-thirds of the country controlled by the Taleban.
Any news of Taleban's advance northward leads to a drop in the value of the afghani there, local traders said.
"The inflation rate in the north and specially in Mazar has gone up to 140 per cent for the past month, while it is 26 per cent in Kabul," Piladini said.
"People have not received their salaries for a long time," Ismael Omar, a World Food Programme official, said.
"The situation is not good for most people. The number of beggars have gone up significantly. A lot of people sleep with empty stomachs in Kabul, but Mazar is far worse."
Aid workers and Taleban authorities in Kabul say the economic sitution in the north was deteriorating daily.
There were reports that people in Kunduz province protesting against high prices last week stoned the office of the provincial governor.
"We hear stories from the north that Dostum's commanders are buying dollars and that is one of the causes for the fluctuation of Dosum's afghani," one aid worker said.
"Markets are full of food, the problem is the access to food for people of the north."
The rate of the afghani in Kabul's money market was 27,000 per dollar at the end of the day on Monday while traders said the rate was 95,000 afghanis to the dollar in Mazar-i-Sharif.
